subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The diathesis-stress model is a good example of interactionism because it states that a disorder results from:
options: A genetic vulnerability triggered by an environmental stressor
questions.explain: Diathesis-stress proposes that an inherited vulnerability (diathesis) is triggered by environmental stress.

questions.q: The idea of 'levels of explanation' suggests that:
options: Only the lowest, biological level is valid
There are several complementary levels, from socio-cultural to neurochemical, for explaining a behaviour
questions.explain: Levels of explanation propose a hierarchy of complementary descriptions, from social to biochemical, for the same behaviour.

questions.q: Ainsworth's Strange Situation has been criticised as ethnocentric because it:
options: Treats the US/Western secure attachment type as the norm for all cultures
questions.explain: The Strange Situation is an 'imposed etic', using US norms of secure attachment as a universal standard.

questions.q: 'Epigenetics' supports the interactionist view because it shows that:
options: The environment can switch genes on or off without changing the DNA sequence
questions.explain: Epigenetics demonstrates that environmental factors alter gene expression without changing the underlying DNA.

questions.q: 'Soft determinism' (associated with the cognitive approach) proposes that:
options: There are no causes of behaviour
Behaviour is determined but people still have some conscious choice within constraints
questions.explain: Soft determinism holds that behaviour is constrained by causes but people can still exercise some conscious choice.

questions.q: A problem for the hard determinist position within the legal system is that:
options: It implies offenders cannot be held morally responsible for their actions
It is identical to soft determinism
It supports the idea of personal responsibility
questions.explain: If behaviour is entirely caused, it is inconsistent with the legal assumption that people freely choose to offend.

questions.q: The nomothetic approach aims to:
options: Establish general laws and norms that apply to all people
questions.explain: The nomothetic approach seeks general laws by studying large samples to produce norms and predictions.

questions.q: An argument that the free will position has practical value is that:
options: Believing one has free will (an internal locus of control) is associated with better mental health
It denies any cause of behaviour
It is more scientific than determinism
questions.explain: Research links a belief in free will/internal locus of control with greater motivation and better mental health.

questions.q: 'Androcentrism' is best defined as:
options: Taking male behaviour/thinking as the norm or standard
questions.explain: Androcentrism treats male behaviour as the standard against which female behaviour is judged, often as a deviation.

questions.q: 'Socially sensitive research' is best defined as studies that:
options: Have potential consequences or implications for the participants or groups they represent
questions.explain: Socially sensitive research has wider social consequences for participants or the social groups they represent.

questions.q: Skinner's view that behaviour is shaped entirely by reinforcement and past conditioning is an example of:
questions.explain: Environmental determinism explains behaviour as the product of external conditioning and reinforcement history.

questions.q: 'Holism' in psychology is the view that:
options: A system must be studied as a whole, as the parts interact to form more than their sum
Behaviour is best understood by breaking it into component parts
questions.explain: Holism argues that behaviour can only be understood by considering the whole, since the parts interact.

questions.q: Beta bias in gender research refers to theories that:
options: Minimise or ignore differences between genders
Assume women are superior to men
questions.explain: Beta bias minimises or ignores differences between the genders, often by assuming findings from one apply to both.

questions.q: Explaining behaviour at the simplest possible level, such as neurochemical activity, is known as:
questions.explain: Reductionism explains behaviour by reducing it to its simplest constituent components.

questions.q: Judging other cultures by the standards and values of one's own culture is known as:
questions.explain: Ethnocentrism is using one's own culture as the benchmark, often viewing other cultures as inferior or abnormal.

questions.q: Alpha bias in psychological research refers to theories that:
options: Exaggerate or overstate differences between genders
Minimise or ignore differences between genders
questions.explain: Alpha bias exaggerates differences between men and women, often presenting them as real and fixed.

questions.q: The view that genes, hormones and brain structure cause behaviour is termed:
questions.explain: Biological determinism explains behaviour as the result of internal physiological factors such as genes and hormones.

questions.q: The idiographic approach to research is characterised by:
options: Focusing in depth on the individual and their unique experience
Seeking general laws that apply to everyone
questions.explain: The idiographic approach studies individuals in depth, treating each as unique rather than seeking general laws.

questions.q: The behaviourist explanation of attachment in terms of stimulus-response associations is an example of:
questions.explain: Environmental reductionism reduces complex behaviour to simple learned stimulus-response links.

questions.q: Universality, the aim of producing findings true for all people regardless of gender or culture, is most undermined by:
options: Gender and culture bias in research
questions.explain: Gender and culture bias threaten universality by producing findings that do not generalise beyond the studied group.

questions.q: The 'interactionist' approach to nature-nurture argues that:
options: Nature and nurture work together and cannot be meaningfully separated
questions.explain: The interactionist position holds that genes and environment interact, making it impossible to separate their effects cleanly.

questions.q: Which research method is most associated with the idiographic approach?
questions.explain: Detailed case studies (e.g. of single patients) are typical of the idiographic approach.

questions.q: Which is an 'ethical implication' that goes beyond standard ethical issues with participants?
options: How findings may be used by policymakers or to justify discrimination
questions.explain: Ethical implications concern the wider impact of findings, such as their use to inform policy or justify prejudice.

questions.q: Explaining OCD purely in terms of low serotonin levels is an example of:
questions.explain: Biological reductionism reduces behaviour to physiological processes such as neurotransmitter activity.

questions.q: 'Cultural relativism' is the view that:
options: Behaviour can only be properly understood within its own cultural context
Differences between cultures should be ignored
questions.explain: Cultural relativism holds that norms and behaviours are meaningful only relative to the culture in which they occur.

questions.q: In the free will versus determinism debate, 'hard determinism' is the view that:
options: Behaviour is partly free and partly determined
All behaviour is caused by factors beyond our control, so free will is an illusion
We have complete free will over all actions
questions.explain: Hard determinism claims all behaviour has a cause and free will is an illusion.

questions.q: A scientific argument FOR determinism in psychology is that it:
options: Is consistent with the scientific aim of establishing cause-and-effect relationships
questions.explain: Determinism fits the scientific approach because it assumes lawful, predictable causes that can be studied empirically.

questions.q: Research suggesting a genetic basis for intelligence is socially sensitive partly because it could be misused to:
options: Justify discriminatory policies such as selective breeding or restricted opportunity
questions.explain: Such findings risk misuse to justify discriminatory or eugenic policies, a key ethical implication.

questions.q: The claim that behaviour is controlled by unconscious conflicts we cannot know about reflects which type of determinism?
questions.explain: Psychic determinism (Freud) attributes behaviour to unconscious drives and early-childhood conflicts.

questions.q: In the nature-nurture debate, the term 'nature' refers to:
questions.explain: 'Nature' refers to inherited, genetically determined influences on behaviour.
